# 09-karsa — sources

Back-test entry `09-karsa.yaml`: Karsa, buying and saving dollar stablecoins where the local currency inflates
(YC Winter 2025). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Karsa (YC W25), 2025-01-30, 215 comments — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42879661 (a comment is cited by its own item URL)
- [LYC] Launch YC: Karsa, the global dollar account — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MgV-karsa-the-global-dollar-account
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/karsa (now "a stablecoin neobank")
- [DAWN23] Dawn, on digital currencies in Pakistan as "a high-tech replacement for hawala-hundi" (headline shortened here), 2023-10-30 — https://www.dawn.com/news/1784968
- [AAJ] Aaj News, "Dollars disappear from open market due to hoarding", 2022-12-15 — https://english.aaj.tv/news/30306930
- [DAWN21] Dawn, "Biometric proof must for buying $500 or above: SBP", 2021-10 — https://www.dawn.com/news/1650577/biometric-proof-must-for-buying-500-or-above-sbp
- [NAYA] NayaPay help, the SBP's annual card limit — https://help.nayapay.com/article/242-what-is-the-annual-card-based-international-transactions-limit-set-by-the-sbp
- [ARAB] Arab News, "Pakistan says has no plans to freeze foreign currency accounts", 2023-06-12 — https://www.arabnews.pk/pakistan/pakistan-says-has-no-plans-to-freeze-foreign-currency-accounts-2320266

## Market

The public material supports **Pakistan** best: the founder's family ([HN] "his uncle in Pakistan"; [LYC] "Shahryar's
family in Pakistan still acutely faces this problem"), the first live sellers ([YCP] "Pakistan, India, Nigeria,
Kenya, Paraguay"), the PKR page discussed in the thread, and the most press on the problem. The segment and all twenty
respondents are in Pakistan. The eval's loader (`instructions/corpus.py`, `MARKET_CURRENCY`) knows only GB, US, IE, FR,
DE, IN, CA and AU, so per the brief the `market` line is **US** (`language: en-US`) and every money value is in USD.
Dollars are also the unit these savers think and buy in (the fee is 1% of the dollars bought). keel-cloud's own
`Market` table does not know PK either, though `Market.chosen` would take PK with an explicit currency.

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** People in Pakistan who earn in rupees and save.
   [HN] "when Shahryar tried explaining [it] to his uncle in Pakistan, it was all jargon until he explained
   stablecoins, which immediately clicked." → `roles[saver]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Keep savings from losing value.
   [HN] "buy and save in stablecoins to protect against currency instability and inflation"; "Over a billion people
   live in countries with severe inflation and are unable to protect their wealth due to strict capital controls."
   → `context.job`, `statements.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When they have rupees left over and want dollars, with the bank and the exchange companies in the
   way. [HN] "earning in a currency thatʼs inflating 20-30% year-over-year"; "good luck getting a foreign currency
   account." [AAJ] dollars "not being readily available in the open market". [DAWN21] exchange companies must "conduct
   biometric verification for all foreign currency sale transactions equivalent to $500 and above". [NAYA] card-based
   international transactions "of up to USD 30,000 per year", "per individual, not per card".
   → `context.circumstance`. Author's choice: the occasion "payday", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out
   of 3, and Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most"): no public figure says how often.

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** [HN] "(1) earning in a currency thatʼs inflating 20-30% year-over-year, (2)
   whoʼs structurally limited from dollar access, and (3) makes payments abroad regularly". → `context.segment`
   (narrowed to Pakistan, the market chosen; condition 3 becomes the Importance rival "Paying for things abroad").

5. **Who pays.** The saver, alone. [HN] "We currently take a 1% transaction fee". → `persona.decision_maker:
   same_person`, Buyer and payer "Nobody else". Author's choice: no other role is named.

6. **Mechanism.** [HN] "Karsa looks and feels like a bank/currency exchange to an average user—they choose an amount
   and buy dollar-denominated stablecoins at a market price. But under the hood, we route our supply from a network of
   verified peer-to-peer stablecoin traders"; "A seller sets their price and deposits money in an escrow smart
   contract"; the buyer "has to send a fiat payment (e.g., bank transfer, payment app, etc.) to the sellerʼs local
   account + upload a photo for verification"; "we ... release the escrowed stablecoins to a digital wallet weʼve
   created for the buyer." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, the Compatibility and Adoption friction items
   (the ID card and payment photo item comes from the same step and from [HN] "we do KYC"). Commitment's step "buy a
   small first amount of dollars" is the author's.

7. **Price.** [HN] "We currently take a 1% transaction fee, though we eventually intend to adjust it proportionally to
   regional FX rates." → `commercial.price` {1, 3, month}: author's arithmetic, 1% of about $100 to $300 of dollars
   bought a month (the amount is the author's choice). Existing sacrifice {5, 15, month}: the premium paid today,
   from [DAWN23] (the PKR-to-USDT premium over the official rate reportedly widened from Rs5-6 to Rs8-9) and [HN] (India:
   "the bid-ask spreads are calamitous - to the tune of 5-6% per side" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42885086),
   taken as 3% to 5% of the same $100 to $300 (author's arithmetic). Ability to pay is derived by code (7% to 60%).

8. **Occasions.** [HN] "Users in these countries already use exchanges like Binance almost like a dollar checking
   account" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42880301 ; a user in Bolivia: "there’s a limit of 50 USD on USD
   transactions per week for each bank" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42881375 (outside the chosen market, so
   it shaped the statement, not a respondent); [DAWN23] "A need for wealth preservation in the face of high inflation and
   currency devaluation"; "a high share of activity happening in Pakistan is through peer-to-peer exchanges".

No respondent carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Open
- Market: the loader knows no PK currency, so the entry is US / en-US with dollars while the segment and every
  respondent are in Pakistan. A Keel study in Pakistan would ask in English or Urdu and might price in rupees; that is
  not tested here.
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds (most had it, most say getting
  savings into dollars is one of their two, today's ways fall short); the solution splits on paying a seller they have
  never met (eight of thirteen would); the commercial side splits on what the problem costs them today (several pay
  little or nothing besides inflation) and on taking a first step, while the 1% fee itself holds. This is the author's
  reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- Two respondents transpose accounts from India (the KYC wall, the spread) to Pakistan; the Bolivian $50-a-week limit
  shaped the founder's statement only.
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are three months' worth.
- DAWN23's headline is shortened in the source list: its first word holds a string banned from these files.
- The amount bought a month ($100 to $300), the occasion "payday", the window and the Prevalence bin are the author's.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Nadia and Farhan do share the bills worry, but the name joins two separate concerns, and Usman's fear of sending money to a stranger online is the same safety worry as Farhan's seller who never released, so leaving him on his own splits one concern in two.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line: all three talk about real worries over saving, even if none names a price.

founder.order_why: Most of it flows well, but the second who-decides question (14, 'besides the saver, who has to agree') comes after the cost and price screens, which splits the who-decides questions (10 and 11) away from it.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 10 and 14: 'would the saver decide and pay or someone else' and 'besides the saver, who has to agree' both ask whether anyone else is involved, and for Karsa the answer is the saver alone both times. Screens 15 and 16 then confirm the same buyer/payer point again. Screens 3 and 4 show the same question twice.
founder.missing: Pakistan could not be chosen as the market, so I sell in PKR but had to say US. The flow never asks the currency, or whether to ask in Urdu. Price only fits as a monthly amount, but Karsa charges a 1% fee on each purchase, so I had to guess a monthly amount bought. Nothing asks about trust in paying a peer-to-peer seller through escrow, or about the ID and payment-photo step, and those are the main frictions for my users.

PRIMARY.order_why: The fee question comes before I'm asked whether I'd buy at all, and it sits under 'What you do today' even though it's about Karsa's price, not what I do now.
PRIMARY.missing: How I actually turn rupees into dollars today (Binance P2P with the back-and-forth chats per trade, or the open market), the premium I pay over the bank rate, how often I do it and roughly how much, and whether dollars were even available when I wanted them.

screens.why1: Naming the project is the obvious first step before Keel turns my idea into a study, so it belongs on screen one.
screens.why2: "What should we call this project?" is plain to any founder on first reading, with no word I would not use.
screens.why3: I know my company's name and what it does, so I can answer at once.
screens.why4: A free-text name box has no options, so there is nothing to be incomplete or overlapping, but it gives no hint whether it wants a bare name or a tagline, and I typed both.
screens.why5: My name and line, "Karsa — save in dollars when your currency keeps falling", are kept as I typed them, and as a founder screen nothing leaks to a respondent.
screens.instead: What should we call this project? (just a short name for you -- the people you ask won't see it)

screens.why1: Right after naming the project, asking where I sell first is the obvious next step, since it sets the currency and language for everything after.
screens.why2: "Where will you sell this first?" is plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly where I'm launching: Pakistan, where my family is, where my first sellers are, and where my rupee-earning savers live.
screens.why4: The true answer, Pakistan, isn't offered; the picker knows only GB, US, IE, FR, DE, IN, CA and AU, so I'm forced onto the US, which is the one place my customers are not.
screens.why5: The screen now records my market as the US, which is wrong: my savers earn in rupees in Pakistan, and every question priced in dollars to 'US' respondents loses that.

screens.why1: Right after I said nobody else has to agree, Keel shows back who has the problem and who decides, so it is the obvious place to check the people before the pricing questions are built on them.
screens.why2: "saver · has the problem" and "saver · decides to buy" are plain, though "buy" reads a little like a purchase when what my user pays is a 1% fee on the dollars they buy, which still fits.
screens.why3: I know who my user is: the person in Pakistan with rupees left over decides alone and pays the fee from their own pocket, exactly as I said.
screens.why4: Two rows, both the saver, match what I typed (same person, nobody else), with no invented role and room to reword or add if I needed to.
screens.why5: The belief "The saver decides, and nobody else has to agree" is what I meant, and no role was added; nothing of Karsa's escrow or sellers leaks onto the rows.

screens.why1: Testing that I alone decide follows naturally from the who-decides answer, but a 'which one do you want to test?' list with only one entry, right after the check screen, feels like an extra click rather than a choice.
screens.why2: The intro says 'pick the one role', yet the only option is 'Nobody else', which isn't a role, and the placeholder bar ('say the one you pick had to agree') contradicts it until I pick, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: I know my savers; whoever has rupees left over at payday decides alone whether to turn them into dollars, so this is squarely inside what I know.
screens.why4: 'Nobody else' is the true answer from my material and the only one offered, but a single-item pick-list framed as roles is an odd set of options.
screens.why5: The belief 'the saver decides, and nobody else has to agree' is mine, but the bar's 'bought an easy way to hold dollars' drifts from what my savers actually do, which is buy dollars.
screens.instead: Skip the list and confirm directly: 'Keel will test: the saver decides alone. Holds if at least 2 in 3 savers say nobody else had to agree the last time they bought dollars with their rupees.'

screens.why1: After who decides and what it costs, asking what first step I'd want a saver to take is the obvious last piece of whether they will pay.
screens.why2: 'First real step' and the hint's 'time, data, money or a signature' are plain to me, and I answered in a few words on first reading.
screens.why3: I know what a first step looks like for my users: they buy a small amount of dollars to try it before trusting it with more.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box and the only chip, 'Leave this out of the study', is the right way out for a founder with no first step in mind.
screens.why5: 'Most savers would buy a small first amount of dollars now' keeps my words; 'most' and 'now' only turn it into a belief to test, and nothing of Karsa's name or escrow leaks.

screens.why1: Right after I picked the first step on screen 17, it's natural to check how Keel wrote it before it goes to strangers.
screens.why2: "Buy a small first amount of dollars" is how a saver in Pakistan would say it, and the step itself is under nine words.
screens.why3: Buying dollars with leftover rupees is exactly what these savers do or want to do, so they can answer from their own life.
screens.why4: This is a card to check and save, with no options, rows or chips.
screens.why5: It no longer says the dollars are bought this new way, from a seller through escrow, so a saver who already buys from a dealer or on Binance would say yes without it telling me anything about my product.
screens.instead: Most savers would buy a small first amount of dollars this new way within the next month.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step, offering to collect the people who would take it is the obvious last thing before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Pilot is a plain word to me as a founder fresh out of YC, and the hint says exactly what respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of Pakistani savers ready to buy dollars through Karsa is my own call to make, and I know the answer at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two are distinct, and nothing is missing for a single switch.
screens.why5: The line drops the step I just typed, 'buy a small first amount of dollars', for a generic 'try this for real', and asks for an email where my savers would more naturally leave a WhatsApp number.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you buy a small first amount of dollars this way? Leave your WhatsApp number or email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my questions belongs here, after the pitch and pilot and just before the study goes out to savers.
screens.why2: I can follow it, but the hint packs video, typing, voice recording, 400 credits and text messages into one long paragraph, so it needs a second read.
screens.why3: I can play each 5-second clip and judge for myself which voice my uncle and people like him would sit through.
screens.why4: Both voices sound like Western English names and nothing offers Urdu or a Pakistani-English voice, which would fit savers in Karachi or Lahore far better.
screens.why5: It still says savers and leaks nothing of Karsa, escrow or stablecoins to the people being asked.
screens.instead: Who should ask savers your questions? Daphne (English) ▶ · Saskia (English) ▶ · A Pakistani voice, in Urdu or English ▶ (400 credits whichever you pick; the link goes by text or WhatsApp)

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the savers, it is obvious I now pick how they answer before the link goes out.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' reads oddly; it is unclear whether something is recording me or the voice is still being made.
screens.why3: I know my savers in Pakistan are mostly on phones, often on patchy data and wary of being on camera about money, so I can judge which format suits them.
screens.why4: The three formats are distinct and complete, but the Daphne option mixes a status note into its text and says nothing about asking aloud in Urdu, which is what would decide it for my people.
screens.why5: Nothing of Karsa's product or roles leaks into the format choice, and my pick 'Read and tap' is kept as I chose it.
screens.instead: How should savers answer? — Read and tap (works on any phone, ready now) / Daphne asks aloud on video, in English (ready in a few minutes) / Let each saver choose when they open the link

screens.why1: Once I've picked how savers answer, the obvious last thing to settle is who gets the link, so this belongs at the end of the send step.
screens.why2: Each option names who gets the link and how in a short line; 'the Contacts page' is Keel's own page, and as the person setting up the study I would know it by now.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I will reach, starting with family and friends-of-family in Pakistan, so I can answer this straight away.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel search and one open link posted where people already are (for me, a WhatsApp group of savers) cover the real choices, and none of them overlap.
screens.why5: Nothing here touches what I typed about savers or Karsa; the screen only asks how the links go out.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits right beside the number that decides it, 'Commitment: 4 of 7 said yes', so I know which card sank the stage and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives the count, the n and the bar, but some need a second look: Existing sacrifice counts over 6 where every other card counts over 7, Ability to pay says 'too few to call' beside '4 of 7 … 5 needed', which reads like a miss, and the numbering skips 5.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer and Commitment are word for word what I checked, but Existing sacrifice has become 'about 1.5% of the rupees they move', not the 3-5% premium I pay today, and price is said in rupees moved where I charge 1% of the dollars bought.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what to do now that commitment fell one short, such as asking the three who wouldn't buy what stops them, or whether the 1% fee or trusting an unknown seller is the issue; the line under the verdict only explains the interview format.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, but no card says seven is a small sample, and 'bigger than you thought' is a soft overstatement for a result that only reached the bar at 4 of 6.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 4 of 7 would buy a first amount of dollars now, one short of the 5 needed; with only 7 answers, read why the 3 held back before changing the fee, since price was also one short.

screens.why_b1: The status line says the belief held and puts 4 of 6 at or above 1.5% beside it, so I know it held and on what count, even if the wording runs ahead of the number.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 4 for and 2 against over 6 against a 4-of-6 bar plainly, but 'above your range' at 1.8% next to 'your low' at 1.5% made me look twice to work out what my range even is.
screens.why_b3: Existing sacrifice is my dimension, but I put what they lose today at 3 to 5% of the dollars bought, the premium over the official rate, not 'about 1.5% of the value of the rupees they are saving', and the question about the 'last rupee leftover' is not how my savers talk.
screens.why_b4: It sends me to the Price card but never sets the cost they named against my 1% fee, which is the one comparison I need from this card.
screens.why_b5: The count line says 'a lean, not a call', but the headline 'bigger than you thought: they lose more today than you estimated' oversells a result sitting exactly at the bar, with 2 of 6 below my low and one 9% answer pulling it up.
screens.instead: Just held, 4 of 6 at the bar: four lose 1.5% or more today and two lose less, a lean from six people. What they lose is above your 1% fee for four of them, so see the Price card next.

screens.why_b1: The status "People disagree" sits right beside "4 of 7 at 1% or more · bar 5 of 7 · 1 short", so I see both the call and the number that makes it.
screens.why_b2: The bands are labelled with for/against, the strip shows 4 for and 3 against out of 7, and the marker sits at 5, so I can read what is counted, over how many and where my bar is.
screens.why_b3: My price is recognisable as a 1% fee, but I charge 1% on the dollars bought per transaction; the card makes it "1% of the rupees they move to dollars a month", and the question asks for "a fee a month", which sounds like a monthly charge.
screens.why_b4: The So line only sends me to the Insights tab; it doesn't say that just one person wanted a lower fee while two would pay no fee at all, so the level of 1% is not what failed.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, "a small group: a lean, not a call" flags the low n, and nothing is called strong.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 accept 1% or more, 1 short of the bar, but only 1 of the 3 against wanted a lower fee; the other 2 won't pay any fee at all, out of trust or no need, so keep 1% per purchase and work on trust, not price.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated, but the numbers beside it disagree: the verdict says 4 of 7 with 5 needed, while the chart and strip show all 4 counted clearing a bar of 3 of 4, so I can't tell which bar decides.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 4 for and the marker at 3, but the axis stops at 3, a ghost cell appears with no explanation, and the chart's bar (3 of 4) differs from the verdict's (5 needed), so it takes a second look to see what is counted and against which bar.
screens.why_b3: The card is recognisably about my 1% fee being paid out of what savers already lose on the dealer premium, but Keel derived this belief and worded it; I did not type it.
screens.why_b4: 'Waits until 5 have' tells me to get one more paying answer, but it never says the useful part: everyone who would pay already loses at least 1%, so the fee comes out of the gain.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible throughout and the small group is flagged as 'a lean, not a call', so nothing claims more than the four answers can carry.
screens.instead: All 4 savers who would pay 1% already lose 1% or more to dealers today, so the fee fits inside what they lose; that is only 4 people, so hear from one more before calling it.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 decided alone · bar 5 of 7", so I see at once that my belief held and by how much it cleared the bar.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who decided alone among the 7 who answered, the strip shows 6 for and 1 against, and the marker sits at 5, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: "Buyer and payer" and "The saver decides, and nobody else has to agree" are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count; it doesn't tell me what to do with it, such as selling straight to the saver with no household or family pitch.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly says the group is small and this is a lean, but the So line then says flatly "They decide alone", and it calls Usman's answer "needed someone's agreement" when he said someone else decided for him.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only a lean with 7 people: 6 of 7 decided alone and 1 had someone else decide for them, so pitch to the saver directly and don't build for a family sign-off yet.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "4 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7 · 1 short", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts answers to the buy-a-first-amount question over the 7 who answered, and the bar at 5 of 7 is stated both as a count and as the 'no more than 1 in 3 against' rule, which agree.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and 'Most savers would buy a small first amount of dollars now' are exactly the dimension and line I checked.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates that 3 of 7 would not buy and sends me to the Insights tab; it doesn't say what this means for the idea, such as making the first step smaller or easier to trust before asking them to pay a seller they've never met.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the screen says plainly that a small group gives a lean, not a call, so the 'did not hold' at one short is not oversold.
screens.instead: One short of the bar with 7 people: a lean against, not a call. The three who said no or probably not balk at the first purchase, so try a smaller or escrow-guaranteed first buy and ask more savers before dropping it.

screens.why_b1: Commitment's 'Did not hold' sits beside 4 of 7 against a bar of 5, but Price is labelled 'People disagree' while its own line says 1 short of the bar, so I have to work out myself that the fee did not clear it either.
screens.why_b3: Commitment is my belief word for word, but Price turns my 1% fee on each purchase into '1% of the rupees they move to dollars a month', which I recognise but did not write.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what these answers mean for Karsa; the only framing is a 'When a line fails · 1 min' header.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, but Commitment shows its question 'What would you start with instead?' over an empty box, which reads as if nobody had an alternative, when in fact two of the three never saw it and one was asked on Price.
screens.why_b6: The quotes give me things I did not type: Farhan lost everything to a seller who never released and Usman's father would veto sending money to a stranger, so the fee objection is really about trusting escrow and the family, and Nadia already has a dollar account.
screens.instead: Price: fell 1 short of your bar, and the three who balked weren't haggling over 1% but don't trust paying a stranger (one lost money to a seller who never released, one family would veto it), so make escrow and seller trust visible before you touch the fee; Commitment: none of the three who said no was asked what they'd start with instead, so ask them.

screens.why1: It is the first screen and checks the one thing the study is about, that I am paid in rupees, so it is obvious why it comes first.
screens.why2: Five plain words; my salary comes in rupees and I would answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know exactly how I am paid, so there is nothing to guess.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it completely, and a gate question has no escape option, which is right here.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'earn in rupees' and says nothing about dollars, Binance or any product, so nothing leaks.
screens.why6: It is one short question that is clearly yes or no when heard, though adding 'Yes or no.' as the screener template does would round it off.

screens.why1: Right after asking if I earn in rupees, showing me the idea before asking about it makes sense, since I already do this kind of swap on Binance P2P.
screens.why2: Stablecoins, escrow and verified seller are the words I use every week on P2P, so I get it on first read, though promising 'no jargon' while saying escrow and stablecoins made me smile.
screens.why3: Turning leftover rupees into dollars by bank transfer or JazzCash to a local seller is exactly what I do now, so I can judge this from my own life.
screens.why4: It is a card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The meaning holds, but the belief line repeats the how almost word for word, including 'with no jargon' a second time, so it reads like the founder's pitch copied in rather than a plain claim about what I would get.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is seven sentences and the last one repeats the whole flow, so by the end I am holding a long pitch rather than one clear idea.
screens.instead: Imagine Karsa, an app to turn leftover rupees into dollars. You pick an amount, pay a checked local seller by bank or mobile wallet, and the app holds their dollars until your payment lands, then puts them in a wallet in your name. The people building it believe this would save you the back-and-forth chats of buying dollars from strangers.

screens.why1: Asking what I lose when I turn my spare rupees into dollars makes sense right after the idea card, but it comes abruptly and the stem is not anchored to a real occasion I can picture, like the last time I bought dollars.
screens.why2: "Your last rupee leftover" is not something I would ever say, "miss" the value is unclear (lost to inflation while I waited, or lost to the open-market premium?), and the label "% of the rupees you move to dollars" asks a different thing from the stem, so I would not know what number to give.
screens.why3: I do know roughly what premium I paid over the bank rate the last time I bought dollars, or how much the rupee fell while I held it, but the question does not say which one, so I would be guessing.
screens.why4: There are three escape chips where only one should exist, "None" overlaps with typing 0, and "I'd rather not say" is a chip the rules say does not exist.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the founder's "they have rupees left over" has drifted into the odd noun "rupee leftover", and "move to dollars" reads like an app's term, not mine.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is a mouthful: the stem goes past twenty words in effect, then "a percent of the rupees you move to dollars, or a low and a high; none is 0" is a second instruction in one breath, and the "%" and the "0" are things the eye reads, not the ear.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you bought dollars with rupees you had saved. About what percent above the bank rate did you pay? Or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: Asking what fee I'd pay makes sense right after the Karsa card, but the header says 'What you do today' when this is about their product, so it lands a bit abruptly.
screens.why2: I know stablecoins and USDT from Binance, but 'a fee a month on what you move' confuses me: on Binance P2P I pay a premium on each conversion, not a monthly percentage, so I'd have to read it twice to work out what the percent is of.
screens.why3: I already pay the P2P premium over the open-market rate every time I turn rupees into dollars, so I can say what cut would feel fair.
screens.why4: The bands go up cleanly without overlaps, cover the range I'd think in, and 'I wouldn't pay a fee' plus 'I can't say' cover the rest.
screens.why5: A fee 'on what you move' that is also charged 'a month' mixes a per-conversion cut with a monthly charge, which drifts from a simple fee on each conversion.
screens.why6: The two-step percent list is easy to hold when heard, but 'Or say you can't say' trips on the ear and 'a fee a month on what you move' is unclear spoken once.
screens.instead: Karsa takes a small cut each time you change rupees into dollars. What cut would feel fair to you? Under half a percent · Half to under 1% · 1% to under 2% · 2% to under 5% · 5% or more · I wouldn't pay a cut; escape: I can't say

screens.why1: Asking who has to agree is plausible for family money, but straight after a fee question it is abrupt, and for my own leftover rupees I would not expect it.
screens.why2: I have to read 'something like this' twice: does it mean buying dollars on Binance P2P, or paying a fee to an app like Karsa?
screens.why3: I can answer about my last time buying dollars, but I have never paid for a service like this, so I would be guessing at what counts.
screens.why4: 'No, someone else decided for me' is an odd answer to 'did anyone else have to agree', and the two 'Yes' options overlap; there is also no family option, which is the real case here.
screens.why5: 'Something like this' points back at Karsa's fee without saying so, so the product drifts into a question that should be about what I do today.
screens.why6: It is one question with four options I can hold, but the options are long and 'Or say you can't say' sounds clumsy when spoken.
screens.instead: The last time you turned your rupees into dollars, did you decide on your own, or did family have a say? Options: I decided on my own; family had to agree; family decided for me. Escape: I can't say.

screens.why1: After the idea, the fee and who has to agree, asking whether I would actually start with a small amount is the natural last question, even if the 'What you do today' kicker does not fit a would-you question.
screens.why2: Buying a small amount of dollars with my leftover rupees is exactly how I think about it, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I decide myself whether to put my own leftover rupees into dollars, so this is my call to make.
screens.why4: There is a 'Probably not' but no 'Probably yes', so the list leans toward no and a hesitant yes like mine has nowhere to go except the full yes.
screens.why5: The card says stablecoins in my wallet but the question says buying dollars, which reads as if I would be getting real dollars, a small drift from what the founder means.
screens.why6: One short question with three short options read as a list I can hold after one hearing.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you buy a small first amount of dollars with it, or not? Yes, I would · Probably yes · Probably not · No
